mission: Japan's AISI was set up after the G7 Hiroshima AI Process to be a hub for AI safety information and evaluation. Director Akiko Murakami describes four activities: building AI-safety benchmarks ('rulers'), being able to evaluate AI models and systems itself, collecting and sharing AI risk information, and leading international cooperation.

key_work.title: Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety
key_work.plain_summary: A guide listing what to check when evaluating the safety of large language model systems, for developers and providers.

key_work.title: Japan AI Safety Institute overview (July 2026)
key_work.plain_summary: Official English overview of J-AISI's background, structure (12 ministries and 5 organisations involved) and activities.

key_work.title: Future direction of AISI from FY2026 (Japanese)
key_work.plain_summary: Murakami's plan: create safety benchmarks with industry, gain in-house evaluation ability, and extend testing from LLMs to AI agents and physical AI.

status_note: launched 14 Feb 2024 inside the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA); designated Japan's central AI-safety institution. In 2026 it plans to double staff to ~60 (Nikkei, Aug 2026), and the government is considering amending the AI Promotion Act (possibly in 2027) to strengthen AISI's role and investigative powers.

size_note: About 30 staff, planned to rise to ~60 by end-2026 and eventually ~200 (Nikkei, 17 Aug 2026).

warnings.text: AI is advancing much faster than earlier technologies, so organisations struggle to keep their risk knowledge current.
Generative AI is increasingly used for cyber attacks; AISI alone cannot handle this and needs cybersecurity partners.
International benchmarks can miss failures specific to Japanese language and culture.

recommendations.text: Build public–private safety benchmarks so government can evaluate AI itself.
Evaluate AI agents and physical AI at the deployment stage, including their harnesses.
Strengthen legal powers to collect information from developers after serious incidents (under discussion in 2026).
